b: Baruch de Espinosa was born in Amsterdam on the twenty fourth of November 1632, in a house on the Houtgracht in the Jewish quarter, close to the warehouses where his father kept dried figs and olive oil. The family were Portuguese Jews. Their grandparents had been made to take Christian names and sit in Christian churches on the Iberian peninsula, and had come north to a city where a person could be Jewish again, more or less, if they were careful.
So the boy grew up among people who already knew, inside their own families, what an opinion could cost. That is the ground everything else grew in.
His mother, Hana Debora, died in November 1638, when he was five. A stepmother, Esther, died in 1653. The house filled and emptied around him while the business carried on.

He was sent to the congregation school, Talmud Torah, and he did well there. Hebrew, Torah, Talmud and the great commentators, taught by men including Saul Levi Morteira, who would later put his name to the document that ruined him. He did not go on to the highest class, the one that made rabbis. The family firm needed hands.

His father Miguel died in March 1654. At twenty one, Baruch was running an import business with his brother Gabriel, and when he looked properly at the books he found more debt in them than goods. In 1656 he went to the Amsterdam orphan court and asked to be released from his father's estate, and he was. He gave up an inheritance rather than keep the appearance of one.
It is the first decision of his life we can document, and it has the shape of every one after it. He preferred the true account to the flattering one, and he was willing to be poorer for it.

b: On the twenty seventh of July 1656 the elders of the Talmud Torah congregation stood in the synagogue and read a writ of herem aloud. The text survives, and it is savage even by the standards of the form. He was cursed by day and by night, cursed sleeping and waking, cut off from Israel. Nobody was to speak with him or write to him, nobody was to do him any service, nobody was to come within four cubits of him, and nobody was to read anything he composed.
He was twenty three years old.

The writ speaks of abominable heresies and monstrous deeds, and then names not one of them. So the honest position is that we do not know what he had said. Later sources offer the likely suspects: that God might have a body, or be nothing other than nature, that the soul is not immortal in the way everyone assumed, that the Law was not handed down as the community claimed. All of it turns up in his later writing. None of it is quoted in the writ.

It helps to see the elders as frightened rather than wicked. They were refugees running a congregation on a permission that could be withdrawn and they had been through this before with Uriel da Costa, excommunicated twice and dead by his own hand in 1640.
Baruch did not recant. He took the Latin form of his name instead, and signed himself Benedictus. Baruch and Benedictus mean the same thing. Blessed.
ch.cap: Elders read the writ of excommunication to the congregation

b: Cut off from one world, he went and learned the language of another. He studied Latin, very probably with Franciscus van den Enden, a former Jesuit who ran a school in Amsterdam, argued for democracy, and was eventually hanged in Paris in 1674 for plotting against Louis the Fourteenth. The company Spinoza kept was not safe company.

With Latin came Descartes, and Descartes was the shock. Here was a philosopher who had thrown out everything he could not see clearly and tried to rebuild from the floor up. Spinoza took the method and refused the conclusions. He would not have two substances, mind and matter, meeting awkwardly somewhere in the middle of the brain. He would not have a free will standing outside the chain of causes.

Then he read Euclid, and found his form. The Elements opens with definitions and axioms that anyone may inspect, proves one proposition at a time, and asks for no trust at all. Spinoza decided to write philosophy that way. His great book has definitions, axioms, propositions, demonstrations and corollaries, in the manner of the geometers.

This was not decoration. He thought rhetoric was how error travels. If a reader is moved by the music of a sentence, the sentence has cheated. Strip the music out, number the steps, and let a person agree because they cannot find the flaw.

In these years he wrote a short treatise on God, man and his well being for a circle of friends, and began an essay on correcting the understanding which he never finished. Around 1661 he left Amsterdam for the village of Rijnsburg, near Leiden.
ch.cap: He builds a philosophy on definitions, axioms and proofs

b: He earned his living grinding and polishing lenses for telescopes and microscopes. It is skilled, patient, physical work: a spinning dish, an abrasive paste, a disc of glass held to a curve measured in fractions of a hair, and a fine dust hanging in the air for hours. Christiaan Huygens, who knew more about lenses than almost anyone alive, thought Spinoza's were excellent.

The trade bought him something he wanted more than comfort. When his friend Simon de Vries tried to make him his heir, he refused, and when the family offered an annuity instead he asked for less than they proposed. He kept his rooms small and his wants smaller, and nobody owned him.

He was not a hermit. Henry Oldenburg, soon to be secretary of the Royal Society in London, came to see him at Rijnsburg in 1661 and wrote to him for years afterwards. Around him gathered a loose circle of Collegiants, Mennonites, physicians and merchants who copied his manuscripts and argued with him by post.

In 1663 he published an exposition of Descartes, the principles of Cartesian philosophy, with a preface by his friend Lodewijk Meyer warning readers that the author did not agree with all of it. It is the only book that appeared under his own name while he lived.

He moved to Voorburg, near The Hague, that same year. And in the room behind the lens wheel the real work was growing: a book that would begin with God and derive from God, in numbered steps, the human mind, the human emotions, human slavery, and the only freedom he thought was on offer.

b: Part one of the Ethics is called Of God, and it moves fast. Substance, he says, is what is in itself and is conceived through itself. If you have to bring in something else to understand a thing, that thing is not substance.

Follow the definition honestly and the plural collapses. Two substances would have to be told apart somehow, and whatever told them apart would limit them, and a limited substance is not in itself. So there is one substance, infinite, with infinitely many attributes, of which the human mind reaches two: thought and extension. Everything else that exists, the North Sea, a lens, a grief, you, is not a thing in its own right but a mode, a particular way this one substance is being.

He calls it God or Nature. The word God is kept, and everything personal in it is removed. This God does not deliberate, does not prefer, does not intervene. Nature follows from the necessity of its own nature the way the angles of a triangle follow from being a triangle. There is no plan, because there is no planner, and no miracle, because there is no outside from which a law could be suspended.

The appendix to part one explains where the plan came from. People find things useful, forget that they are the ones doing the valuing, and conclude that the things were made for them. Eyes for seeing, rain for crops. Then a roof falls on a good man, and rather than give up the story they hide the problem inside the will of God, which Spinoza calls the sanctuary of ignorance.

The hardest consequence is the one about you. Your will is not free. It is caused, by your body, your history and the state of the world. You do choose, your choosing has causes, and the uncaused chooser you feel yourself to be is not there. Most readers stop at this point. Notice what is offered in exchange: you are no longer guilty for having been caused.
ch.cap: One substance: nature unfolding by its own necessity

b: Part two asks what you are, and the answer is one of the most elegant things in philosophy. Mind and body are not two items in a relationship. They are one item, described twice. The same stretch of nature, taken under the attribute of thought, is a mind, and taken under the attribute of extension, is a body.

So there is no puzzle about how a thought pushes an arm, because the thought and the movement are the same event in two vocabularies. The order and connection of ideas, he writes, is the same as the order and connection of things. A mind is the idea of its body, which carries a blunt implication: how much you can think depends on how much your body can do and undergo.

He then sorts knowing into three kinds. There is what we pick up from hearsay and from things merely happening to us, which leaves confused ideas behind. There is reason, which works from what is common to many things and gets reliable results by argument. And there is intuition, which sees a thing's necessity in one movement, the way you see at a glance why a proportion must hold instead of cranking the rule.

In 1670 he interrupted the Ethics and published, anonymously and with a false Hamburg imprint, the theological and political treatise. It reads Scripture as a historical document, written by human beings in a human language at particular times. Moses did not write all five books. Prophets had vivid imaginations, not superior physics. Miracles are the names we give to causes we have not found.
And it argues for the thing he wanted most: that a state exists so that people may think what they like and say what they think. The synods raged, and in 1674 the States of Holland banned the book.
ch.cap: A single event read as thought and as body together

b: Part three opens with an insult to almost everyone who had written on the subject. They treat a human being, he says, as a kingdom within a kingdom, a little sovereign sitting outside nature and disturbing its laws rather than following them. He proposes instead to consider hatred, anger and envy exactly as he would consider lines, planes and solids.

The engine is one word. Conatus. Each thing strives, as far as it is able, to persevere in its own being, and that striving is nothing other than what the thing actually is. Not a duty. Not a virtue. A description.

From there he needs only three basic affects. Desire, which is striving become conscious. Joy, which is the passage to a greater power of acting. Sadness, which is the passage to a lesser one. Love is joy with the idea of an outside cause attached, hatred is sadness with the same. Everything else is built from those pieces: hope, fear, pity, pride, shame, jealousy and ambition, each defined and derived.

Some of the definitions land like a slap. Fear is sadness about something future we are not certain of. Hope is joy about something future we are not certain of. They are the same condition in different coats, both of them symptoms of not knowing, and neither of them a virtue.

The practical gift of part three is this. Your feelings are not failures of character. They are events with causes, and they behave lawfully. Anyone who has ever seriously tried to change themselves will recognise that as the first useful thing anybody said.

b: Part four is called Of Human Bondage, and its central result is the most useful sentence Spinoza wrote. An affect cannot be restrained or removed except by an affect contrary to it, and stronger than it. Not by knowing better. Not by resolve. A bare true idea has no force against a live feeling. Only another feeling moves you, so the work is to make the better feeling the stronger one, by understanding it and by arranging a life in which it is fed.

He also clears out good and evil. They are not properties of the world, they are relations to a striving. What is good is what increases your power to act. Virtue and power, in his hands, are the same word. And because nothing in nature is more useful to a person than another person living by reason, the reasonable life turns out to be a shared one rather than a retreat.

Then comes his portrait of the free man, who acts rather than reacts, keeps faith, declines the favours of the ignorant, and of whom he writes that a free man thinks of death least of all things, and that his wisdom is a meditation upon life, not upon death.

He wrote that in the worst year his country had. In 1672 France invaded and the Republic nearly fell, and on the twentieth of August a mob in The Hague seized Johan and Cornelis de Witt and tore them apart in the street. Leibniz later reported Spinoza telling him that he had wanted to go out that evening and fix up a placard reading ultimi barbarorum, the utmost of barbarians, and that his landlord locked the door and kept him alive. The story is second hand, recalled years afterwards.

The next year he crossed the lines to the French camp at Utrecht and came home suspected of treason, with a crowd gathering at his lodging. That same year Heidelberg offered him a professorship with freedom to philosophise, provided he did not disturb the established religion. He wrote back on the thirtieth of March and declined. He had never wished to teach in public, and he could not see where that proviso ended. He finished the Ethics and put it in a drawer.
ch.cap: His landlord locks the door against the mob outside
ch.h: Bondage, and the year of disaster

b: Part five is the payoff, and the strangest part of the book. If an emotion is a confused idea of something happening to us, then forming a clear idea of it changes what it is. You cannot delete a feeling, but you can convert it, because the confusion it was partly made of is gone. Understand completely why you are angry, and the anger is no longer the same event.

Push that as far as it goes and you arrive at what he calls the intellectual love of God. Love of the whole thing as it actually is, necessary and impersonal, with no expectation of being loved in return. And then at the claim most readers cannot follow, that in grasping things through their necessity, something of the mind is not bound to time. We feel and know by experience that we are eternal, he writes. He is not promising that you will go on, as yourself, remembering.
The last line of the book is a warning rather than a promise. But all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare.

He had the Ethics ready around 1675 and then stopped, hearing that the theologians were moving against him. Leibniz came to talk with him in 1676. On the twenty first of February 1677 he died in his lodging in The Hague, aged forty four, of a lung disease that years of glass dust had not helped. His writing desk was shipped to his publisher in Amsterdam, and his friends had the posthumous works in print before the year was out. The States of Holland banned them in 1678.

For a century afterwards, Spinozist simply meant atheist and was used to end careers. Then in 1785 Jacobi published Lessing's admission that he had been one, and the quarrel that followed put Spinoza at the centre of German philosophy. Einstein, asked whether he believed in God, said he believed in Spinoza's.

Where he is challenged: many readers think calling nature God keeps the comfort of the word while quietly dropping its content. His necessitarianism leaves nothing genuinely able to have gone otherwise, which is hard to square with how we actually deliberate. And part five's eternity of the mind is widely judged his weakest work, the philosopher Jonathan Bennett calling it an unmitigated disaster. What has aged best is the part he thought least metaphysical. One nature, one person, body and mind described twice, and feelings that obey laws you can learn.

note: The dates here come from the surviving record: the writ of herem of July 1656, which is preserved in the congregation's register and names no specific charge, the Principles of Cartesian Philosophy of 1663, the Theological-Political Treatise of 1670 and its ban in 1674, the letter of 30 March 1673 declining the Heidelberg chair, and the Opera Posthuma of 1677. The famous story of an attempted stabbing outside a theatre is left out here, because it rests on Colerus writing from hearsay decades later. The ultimi barbarorum placard comes from Leibniz recalling a conversation years afterwards, and is flagged as second hand in the narrative. Later readers have pressed hardest on part five, where the eternity of the mind is widely judged the book's weakest argument, and on whether identifying God with nature keeps the word while abandoning its meaning.
recall: What exactly happened to Spinoza on 27 July 1656?

The elders of Amsterdam's Talmud Torah congregation read a writ of herem against him, cutting him off from the community. Nobody was to speak with him, come within four cubits of him, or read anything he wrote. He was twenty three, and the surviving writ names no specific charge.
What does Spinoza mean by God or Nature?

He argues that there can only be one substance, so God and nature are the same thing under two names. This God does not deliberate or intervene; it follows from the necessity of its own nature, the way a triangle's angles follow from being a triangle.
What is conatus, and why does part three need it?

Conatus is the striving of each thing to persevere in its own being, which Spinoza says is the thing's actual essence. Every affect is derived from it. Desire is that striving made conscious, joy is a passage to greater power of acting, and sadness a passage to less.
What is Spinoza's rule about restraining an emotion?

An affect can only be restrained or removed by a contrary affect that is stronger than it. Reason on its own has no leverage, because a true idea carries no force. Change therefore means strengthening a better feeling, not resolving harder.
Why was the Ethics not published in Spinoza's lifetime?

He had it ready around 1675 but withheld it, because his anonymous theological and political treatise of 1670 had provoked the Dutch synods and was banned in 1674. He died in February 1677, friends printed the posthumous works that year, and the States of Holland banned them in 1678.
take: An emotion only yields to a stronger emotion
Stop trying to out argue a feeling. Find the rival feeling that points where you want to go, and feed it with attention, company and routine until it is the stronger of the two.
Understanding a feeling changes the feeling
When something has hold of you, write out its real causes until the account is complete. The grip loosens, because a confused idea was part of what the feeling was made of.
Ask what increases your power to act
Judge a habit, a job or a friendship by whether it leaves you more able to do things, rather than by whether it sounds virtuous. That is a question you can answer honestly.
Hope and fear are the same ignorance
Both are unsteady feelings about an uncertain future. When you notice either one, the useful move is to go and find out, not to feel harder.
Spinoza ground lenses so that no patron could tell him what to publish. Keep your costs low enough that your real work is never for sale.
Nothing is more useful to you than another reasonable person
His conclusion from pure self interest is cooperation. Build a small circle of people who will argue with you in good faith, and keep it in repair.
Number your steps when the subject is contested
Set out your definitions, then your claims, then why each one follows. It is slower, and it turns disagreement into something specific instead of something loud.
Expect excellence to be rare and difficult
He ended his masterwork by admitting that almost nobody would manage it. Treat difficulty as evidence that you are in the right place, not proof that you are wrong.
title: The Lens Grinder Who Rebuilt God
wiifm: You will learn how to take a feeling apart without shame and put it back together with more power than it had before. Spinoza hands you a universe with no plan in it, nobody watching and nothing owed to you, and then shows why that is the most freeing news you could be given. You get a method for turning dread into understanding, a test for whether a person is actually free, and a working explanation of why willpower keeps losing. By the end you will see why a lens grinder thrown out of his own community has outlasted almost everybody who threw him.
